executive_summary: This relationship is running on fumes masquerading as fuel. Sam shows up just enough to keep you tethered—a few 'I miss you' texts, apologies for going quiet, promises to call later—but vanishes when it's time to follow through. You're doing all the emotional labor while he operates entirely on his own timeline, comfortable with you waiting and accommodating while he dips in and out like someone checking their phone between meetings.

relationship_energy.label: Barely Present & Cyclical
relationship_energy.summary: The energy here is barely a pulse. Sam reaches out sporadically with maintenance texts like 'hey, how was your day' and 'I miss you,' but these go nowhere. His initiations are almost exclusively last-minute invitations, schedule changes, or low-effort check-ins that evaporate. The pattern isn't rising or stable—it's cyclical: brief flickers of contact, then retreat.

warmth.evidence: Zero emojis, zero exclamation marks across 150 messages; 'I miss you' appears ten times but feels performative without elaboration.

responsiveness.evidence: Median response time 15 minutes, but content is hollow; 'ok' appears fifteen times as his go-to response to everything.

consistency.evidence: 'Sorry went quiet, work is a lot' (nine instances); 'will confirm later' (nine times) followed by 'not sure I can make it' (eight times).

initiation_balance.evidence: Initiates 50% of conversations, but almost exclusively with last-minute 'you free tonight?' or cancellations like 'can we move saturday?'

signals.description: He says 'I miss you' ten times and 'been thinking about what you said' nine times, but never elaborates or creates space for deeper connection.
signals.evidence: 'I miss you' (ten instances); 'been thinking about what you said' (nine instances) with zero follow-up.

signals.description: He proposes connection ('you free tonight?', 'call you after dinner') but immediately follows with cancellations or vagueness.
signals.evidence: 'You free tonight?' (five instances) followed by 'not sure I can make it' (eight times); 'will confirm later' (nine times).

signals.description: He repeatedly thanks you for understanding his absences, which is appreciation for your patience rather than genuine investment.
signals.evidence: 'Thanks for understanding' appears nine times; no reciprocal effort to change behavior.

interest_signals.summary: Sam's investment is primarily in managing your expectations, not building connection. His primary concrete action is proposing plans, but these are almost always followed by cancellations or 'will confirm later' responses. The phrase 'thanks for understanding' appears nine times—he's appreciating your patience while doing the bare minimum. There are no signals of future planning, vulnerability, or genuine curiosity about your life.

question_asking.description: Asks surface-level 'how was your day?' but never waits for answers or builds on responses; zero follow-up questions.

communication_dynamic.response_pattern: Median response time is 15 minutes, but consistency means nothing when content is hollow. He initiates contact sporadically, then disappears for days. When you ask direct questions like 'what time?' or 'are we still on?', he often doesn't answer at all.
communication_dynamic.summary: Sam's communication is functional, not relational. His messages average 6 words—short, transactional, emotionally flat. Zero emojis, zero exclamation marks. His 'apologies' are explanations designed to prevent accountability: 'sorry went quiet, work is a lot' (nine instances) names the reason but never commits to changing behavior. He doesn't ask follow-up questions, doesn't build on your responses, and uses 'ok' as his default reply to everything. There's no humor, no warmth, no curiosity. When you ask 'what time?' or 'are we still on?', the conversation often dies because he's not actually trying to build something—just checking a box labeled 'contacted her today.'

emotional_depth.openness: Closed; he shares only surface-level excuses like 'work is a lot' with no genuine vulnerability.
emotional_depth.supportiveness: Minimal; he doesn't ask how you're doing or offer emotional support beyond 'ok' responses.
emotional_depth.emotional_availability: Unavailable in the literal sense; he won't make himself present to actually be with you emotionally.
emotional_depth.vulnerability_comfort: None; he never shares what he's feeling, thinking, or struggling with beyond work stress.
evidence: 'I would rather we talk properly' (six instances) met with 'ok' (fifteen times) with no curiosity about what you need.
'Been thinking about what you said' (nine instances) with zero elaboration on what he's actually thinking.
emotional_depth.summary: There is almost no emotional depth here. Sam expresses vague longing—'I miss you'—but it feels performative, like he knows it's what you want to hear. He never shares what he misses about you specifically, what he's feeling, or what's happening in his inner world beyond 'work is a lot.' You've asked 'I would rather we talk properly' six times; his response is consistently 'ok' with no effort to create that space. He's not vulnerable, not open, barely present. The phrase 'been thinking about what you said' could indicate emotional processing, but he never tells you what he's thinking—it's another placeholder suggesting engagement without actual engagement.

evidence: Repeated disappearances ('sorry went quiet') followed by vague promises ('will confirm later') are textbook deactivating strategies.
Pattern of proposing connection then backing away: 'you free tonight?' immediately followed by 'can we move saturday?' or 'not sure I can make it.'
attachment_indicators.summary: Sam shows classic avoidant attachment: he maintains emotional distance while keeping you just close enough to feel like there's still a relationship. His repeated disappearances, vague promises, and comfort with leaving you uncertain are deactivating strategies. Avoidant individuals often feel suffocated by expectations and retreat when relationships demand presence. The 15% anxious shows up in intermittent 'I miss you' messages—likely moments when he feels the relationship slipping and needs to pull you back in, not because he's ready to show up, but because he wants the security of knowing you're still waiting. The 10% secure is generous, based only on occasional initiations and 'thanks for understanding'—but secure attachment requires consistent availability, emotional honesty, and follow-through, which Sam offers none of.

flags.description: 'I miss you' appears ten times. In a healthier relationship, this would be beautiful. It shows he's aware something is missing, even if he won't do the work to close that gap.
flags.evidence: 'I miss you' (ten instances) throughout the message thread.

green_flags.summary: Sam has thin green flags. He verbalizes missing you and acknowledges your concerns, showing basic awareness that something matters. He does attempt to initiate plans occasionally, suggesting moments where he wants your company. In this landscape of minimal engagement, these are the smallest seeds of connection—but they're overshadowed by his inability to follow through on any of them.

areas.title: Chronic Unreliability
areas.description: He proposes plans repeatedly but cancels or goes vague almost as often. 'Not sure I can make it' (eight times), 'will confirm later' (nine times), and 'can we move saturday?' (ten times) create a pattern where you can never count on him.
areas.evidence: 'You free tonight?' followed by 'not sure I can make it'; 'will confirm later' with no follow-up.

areas.title: Emotional Unavailability Masked as Busyness
areas.description: 'Work is a lot' (nine instances) is his shield. He uses external circumstances to justify his absence rather than examining his capacity for relationship.
areas.evidence: 'Sorry went quiet, work is a lot' (nine instances); 'long day' repeated without elaboration.

areas.title: Pattern of Accepting Your Accommodation Without Reciprocating
areas.description: He's learned he can maintain the relationship through your grace without changing his behavior. 'Thanks for understanding' (nine times) is him appreciating your patience, not committing to presence.
areas.evidence: 'Thanks for understanding' (nine instances); 'no worries at all' (sixteen times from you) met with continued cancellations.

caution_areas.summary: Three significant patterns demand attention. His chronic unreliability—proposing plans then backing away—teaches him canceling has no consequences. His emotional unavailability masked as work stress prevents real intimacy. Most concerning: he's learned he can maintain the relationship through your accommodation without reciprocating effort. You're doing all the emotional labor while he operates on his own timeline.

reflections.pattern: Over-functioning as the relationship's safety net
reflections.description: Your repeated 'I am here when you want' (eight times), 'no worries at all' (sixteen times), and 'let me know when you can' (ten times) keeps this relationship alive while he does the bare minimum.
reflections.evidence: 'No worries at all' (sixteen times); 'I am here when you want' (eight times); 'let me know when you can' (ten times).
reflections.suggestion: For one week, match his energy exactly. If he sends 'will confirm later,' respond 'okay' and do not follow up. Let him come to you. See what happens when you stop compensating for his withdrawal.

reflections.pattern: Asking questions he won't answer, then accepting the silence
reflections.description: 'Are we still on?' (seven times) and 'What time?' (five times) are reasonable questions that deserve answers. When he ignores them, you move on to the next exchange without addressing the dismissal.
reflections.evidence: 'Are we still on?' (seven instances); 'What time?' (five times) with no response.
reflections.suggestion: Next time he ignores a direct question, say: 'When I ask you a direct question and don't hear back, I feel dismissed. I need you to either answer or tell me you need time to figure it out.' Then stop asking questions twice and observe what he does.

reflections.pattern: Trying to force depth in a shallow dynamic
reflections.description: 'I would rather we talk properly' (six times) is you requesting something he's shown he can't or won't give. You keep asking for the same thing and accepting the same non-response.
reflections.evidence: 'I would rather we talk properly' (six instances) met with 'ok' or silence.
reflections.suggestion: Stop requesting something he's shown he won't provide. Instead say: 'I need deeper conversations to feel connected. If that's not something you can offer right now, I need to know so I can decide what works for me.' Make it about your needs, not fixing him.

your_patterns.overall_theme: You're carrying the full emotional weight of this relationship—maintaining warmth, asking questions, accommodating cancellations, and repeatedly requesting deeper connection while he operates on his own timeline.
your_patterns.summary: You're over-functioning as this relationship's safety net. Your repeated reassurances ('no worries at all', 'I am here when you want') teach Sam that his unreliability has no consequences. You ask direct questions ('are we still on?', 'what time?') that go unanswered, then accept the silence without addressing the dismissal. You've asked for deeper conversation six times and keep accepting 'ok' as a response. You're trying to force intimacy in a dynamic where he's shown he won't meet you there. The pattern is clear: you're doing all the emotional labor while he dips in and out. Your role is to stop compensating for his withdrawal and start holding boundaries around what you actually need.

growth_roadmap.roadmap_intro: You can't create a relationship with someone who's only half-present. You've been bending yourself into accommodating shapes, hoping your patience will inspire his consistency. It won't. Sam's availability isn't about your worthiness—it's about his capacity, and right now, his capacity is limited. The growth here isn't about fixing him; it's about reclaiming your own life and deciding what you're willing to accept.

leverage_areas.title: Reclaim Your Own Availability
leverage_areas.narrative: You've made yourself endlessly available to someone who treats your time as optional. This teaches him that canceling, going quiet, and leaving you uncertain has no consequences. He gets the comfort of knowing you're waiting without the discomfort of showing up consistently. Start protecting your time the way you'd protect a friend's. When he texts 'you free tonight?' at the last minute, say 'I've made other plans—I need more notice.' When he says 'will confirm later,' respond 'I'll plan to be free if I hear from you by [specific time]. Otherwise I'm going to make other plans'—then actually make other plans. Go see friends, pursue your own life, stop orienting your schedule around his maybes. Build in natural consequences: 'I love seeing you, and I need reliability. Going forward, I'm only going to hold space for plans we've both confirmed at least a day ahead.'
actionable_steps: Next time he proposes last-minute plans, respond: 'I'd love to see you, but I need more notice. Can we plan for [specific day/time]?'
Make one standing weekly commitment with a friend that can't be moved, so you have a genuine conflict when he texts last-minute.
When he says 'will confirm later,' set a deadline: 'I need to know by 5pm so I can plan accordingly.' Then actually make other plans if you don't hear back.

leverage_areas.title: Stop Interpreting His Words as Commitments
leverage_areas.narrative: He says 'I miss you' and 'been thinking about what you said,' and you hear meaning. But words without action are just words. He's learned he can maintain the relationship through verbal gestures without behavioral follow-through. Start listening to his actions as the primary language. When he says 'call you after dinner,' your new internal response is: 'I'll believe it when my phone rings.' Don't rearrange your evening, don't sit waiting, don't ask 'did you still want to call?' Just live your life. If he calls, great. If he doesn't, you already knew the words were empty. Practice this: when he says something sweet, respond with 'I appreciate you saying that. What I really need is [specific action]. Can you do that?' Watch what he does with direct requests for behavior, not just words.

growth_roadmap.emotional_habit_to_reduce: Stop cushioning his impact on you with 'no worries at all.' Start naming your actual experience. When he cancels: 'I'm disappointed. I was looking forward to this.' When he goes quiet: 'I felt confused when I didn't hear from you.' When he's vague: 'I need clarity.' You don't have to be harsh—just honest. Right now you're absorbing his unreliability like it doesn't hurt. It does. Let him see that.
growth_roadmap.communication_upgrade: Replace reassurance with requests. Instead of 'I am here when you want' → 'I'd like to see you Wednesday at 7pm. Does that work?' Instead of 'let me know when you can' → 'I need an answer by tomorrow so I can plan accordingly.' Instead of 'are we still on?' → 'I'm planning to be there at 7 unless I hear otherwise by 5pm.' Make him actually commit or decline, not live in the murky middle where he's comfortable.
growth_roadmap.boundary_reinforcement: Propose one weekly anchor—a standing plan that happens the same time every week unless actively canceled 24 hours ahead. 'Let's do Sunday dinner together every week. 7pm, your place or mine. If something comes up, we let each other know by Saturday evening. Otherwise, it's on.' See if he can sustain one predictable commitment. If he can't, you have everything you need to know about his capacity for relationship right now.

key_milestones: Repeated requests for deeper conversation ('I would rather we talk properly' six times) met with 'ok' and silence—intimacy attempts rejected.
Pattern of proposed plans followed by cancellations establishing that commitment means nothing—trust eroding.
relationship_trajectory.look_ahead: In the next 1-3 months, one of two things happens: either you get exhausted from carrying the full weight and walk away, or you resign yourself to this being what the relationship is—sporadic, surface-level, entirely on his terms—and your resentment grows quietly in the background. The trajectory only changes if you have a clarifying conversation and he demonstrates sustained behavioral change over two weeks.
relationship_trajectory.summary: This relationship is heading toward slow erosion. You're pouring energy into maintaining something he's letting atrophy through neglect. The one action that changes trajectory: have the clarifying conversation—in person or on a real phone call. Say: 'I care about you, and I need more consistency and presence than I'm experiencing right now. I need to know if you actually have space in your life for a relationship, or if what you're able to offer right now is casual check-ins. Neither is wrong, but I need to know what this is so I can decide if it works for me.' Then listen to what he says and watch what he does over the next two weeks. If he says he wants the relationship but nothing changes, you have your answer. If he says he's overwhelmed and can't give you what you need, believe him—it's the most honest he's been. If he shows up differently, consistently, for two straight weeks, then maybe he heard you. But here's the truth: you can't negotiate someone into being ready for you. You can only decide what you're willing to accept.
